elements.element: Customer has no most-favoured-nation obligation benefiting Vendor.
elements.evidence: Rendered § 7.2 now reads: "Customer has no obligation to disclose, match, or extend to Vendor any more favourable commercial offer or terms available to a third party." The original disclose-and-match obligation ("Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives") is gone, and § 12.3 independently confirms "Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer ... commitment", so the two provisions are now consistent rather than contradictory. No Vendor-granted MFN in our favour existed to be disturbed.

elements.element: The Customer MFN covers only a defined product.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: after the edit there is no Customer-side MFN at all (§ 7.2 affirmatively disclaims any duty to disclose, match, or extend third-party terms), so there is no scope to confine to a defined product. The preferred outcome subsumes this fallback limit.

elements.element: The Customer MFN lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no Customer MFN survives in the operative text, so no duration limit is required. The 12-month/defined-product structure is offered only in the margin comment as a negotiating fallback, which is appropriate since it is not needed to reach a complete level.

elements.element: The Customer MFN contains reasonable like-for-like comparison carve-outs.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: with the matching obligation deleted there is no comparison mechanic to carve out. § 12.3's acknowledgment of no most-favoured-customer commitment reinforces that no comparison duty remains.

elements.element: Vendor-granted MFN in Customer's favour is retained.
elements.evidence: Not part of the supplied checklist but relevant to the redline guidance ("keep any Vendor-granted MFN"): the edit touches only the Customer-side obligation in § 7.2 and leaves § 12.3 verbatim; nothing beneficial to Customer was removed.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete: the sole preferred element is delivered in operative language, not merely promised in the comment — § 7.2 as rendered affirmatively negates any disclose/match/extend duty running to Vendor.

Fallback elements are vacuously met because the stronger preferred outcome (no Customer MFN whatsoever) removes the conditional predicate; the defined-product/12-month/like-for-like package is correctly held back in the comment as a concession rather than drafted into the text.

Minimal: only the offending sentence in § 7.2 was replaced; § 12.3 and all other allocation, timing, remedy and pricing mechanics are untouched, and no new obligations outside the checklist were introduced. A bare deletion of § 7.2 would have been marginally leaner given that § 12.3 already records that Customer made no most-favoured-customer commitment, but the short declaratory replacement is consistent with § 12.3 rather than duplicative of an operative obligation and avoids leaving a bare section number.

Preserves intent: the edit is one-directional (it removes a burden on us, adds none on Vendor), does not disturb any Vendor-granted MFN (none exists), and cures the internal inconsistency between old § 7.2 and § 12.3.
Comment complies with tone requirements: first person plural, two sentences of explanation plus an express fallback offer, cites the playbook position and § 12.3, no lecturing.

Severity: the rule is catalogued medium, but the original § 7.2 was an open-ended obligation to disclose and match any more favourable third-party offer with no product, term or comparison limits — the stated walk-away — so the finding warrants elevation to high for negotiation priority.
